abstract: <jats:title>Summary</jats:title><jats:p>Multiparental cross designs for mapping quantitative trait loci (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">QTL</jats:styled-content>) provide an efficient alternative to biparental populations because of their broader genetic basis and potentially higher mapping resolution. We describe the development and deployment of a recombinant inbred line (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RIL</jats:styled-content>) population in durum wheat (<jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">T</jats:styled-content>riticum turgidum</jats:italic> ssp. <jats:italic>durum</jats:italic>) obtained by crossing four elite cultivars. A linkage map spanning 2664 cM and including 7594 single nucleotide polymorphisms (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">SNP</jats:styled-content>s) was produced by genotyping 338 <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RIL</jats:styled-content>s. <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">QTL</jats:styled-content> analysis was carried out by both interval mapping on founder haplotype probabilities and <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">SNP</jats:styled-content> bi‐allelic tests for heading date and maturity date, plant height and grain yield from four field experiments. Sixteen <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">QTL</jats:styled-content> were identified across environments and detection methods, including two yield <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">QTL</jats:styled-content> on chromosomes 2<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">BL</jats:styled-content> and 7<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AS</jats:styled-content>, with the former mapped independently from the photoperiod response gene <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">P</jats:styled-content>pd‐<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">B</jats:styled-content>1,</jats:italic> while the latter overlapped with the vernalization locus <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">VRN</jats:styled-content>‐<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">A</jats:styled-content>3</jats:italic>. Additionally, 21 <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">QTL</jats:styled-content> with environment‐specific effects were found. Our results indicated a prevalence of environment‐specific <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">QTL</jats:styled-content> with relatively small effect on the control of grain yield. For all traits, functionally different <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">QTL</jats:styled-content> alleles in terms of direction and size of genetic effect were distributed among parents. We showed that <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">QTL</jats:styled-content> results based on founder haplotypes closely matched functional alleles at known heading date loci. Despite the four founders, only 2.1 different functional haplotypes were estimated per <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">QTL</jats:styled-content>, on average. This durum wheat population provides a mapping resource for detailed genetic dissection of agronomic traits in an elite background typical of breeding programmes.</jats:p>
title: A multiparental cross population for mapping QTL for agronomic traits in durum wheat (Triticum turgidum ssp. durum)
